style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: The book closes with two voices, both finally a mother's. First comes the oracle King Lemuel's mother pressed upon him (vv. 1-9): a queen's charge to a son who will rule -- guard your strength, refuse the wine that makes a judge forget the law, and open your mouth for the voiceless and the poor. Then the book ends where it began, with wisdom embodied in a woman: an acrostic poem (vv. 10-31), each of its twenty-two lines opening with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, A to Z, a complete portrait of the valiant woman whose worth outruns rubies. She is not a quiet ornament but chayil -- 'valor,' the very word used of an army -- a strong, industrious, generous, God-fearing builder of a household. The closing verse sends her works themselves to praise her in the public gates, answering the whole book's question: where is wisdom found? Here, in a life that fears the LORD.

1.text: The words of King Lemuel -- the weighty oracle his mother pressed upon him as she shaped him:
1.amp: The words [dabar] of King Lemuel -- the oracle [massa -- a burden, a load laid on the heart, a weighty pronouncement] that his mother [em] taught and corrected [yasar -- disciplined, instructed, formed by chastening] him.
1.notes: massa (H4853) means both 'burden' and 'oracle' -- a divine word heavy enough to carry; yasar (H3256) is the same disciplining/forming verb behind musar (the prologue's word for corrective instruction in 1:2,8). This closing teaching, like the book's first, comes through a parent shaping a child -- here a queen-mother forming a king.

2.text: What shall I say, my son? What, O son of my womb? What, O son of my vows?
2.amp: What, my son? What, son of my womb [beten -- belly, the innermost place where life is carried]? What, son of my vows [neder -- a sacred promise made to God]?
2.notes: the threefold cry rises in intensity: from 'my son' to 'son of my body' to 'son of my vows.' neder (H5088) recalls a Hannah-like dedication (1 Sam 1:11) -- this child was promised to God before he was given, and the mother's charge flows from that vow.

3.text: Do not pour out your strength on women, nor your ways on those who bring kings to ruin.
3.amp: Do not give [natan] your strength [chayil -- might, valor, the same word later praised in the valiant woman] to women [ishshah], nor your ways [derek] to that which wipes kings out [machah -- blots out, erases, obliterates].
3.notes: chayil (H2428) is a king's vigor and capability; machah (H4229) is to blot out or erase (the word for wiping a dish, Isa 14:23). The warning frames the whole oracle: squandered strength and the appetites that erase a throne -- the same chayil here misspent becomes, in v. 10, a woman's crowning virtue.

4.text: It is not for kings, Lemuel -- it is not for kings to be drinking wine, nor for rulers to crave strong drink.
4.amp: It is not for kings [melek], O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink [shatah] wine [yayin], nor for princes [to ask] 'Where [ay] is strong drink [shekar -- intoxicating drink, beer]?'
4.notes: shekar (H7941) is potent fermented drink, distinct from yayin (H3196), wine. The point is not abstinence as such but the unfitness of a ruler ruled by his thirst -- a king who craves the cup cannot be trusted with the scales of judgment (v. 5).

5.text: Lest he drink, and forget what the law decrees, and twist the just cause of all the afflicted.
5.amp: Lest he drink [shatah] and forget [shakach -- let slip from memory, neglect] what is decreed [chaqaq -- engraved, inscribed as law], and pervert the cause [din -- the legal plea, the right judgment] of all the sons of affliction [oni -- poverty, misery].
5.notes: chaqaq (H2710) is to engrave or inscribe -- law cut into stone, not to be blurred by a fogged mind; din (H1779) is a legal cause or verdict. Wine makes a judge forget the very statutes he is sworn to keep, and the first to suffer are the afflicted who have no other defender.

6.text: Give strong drink to the one perishing, and wine to those bitter in soul.
6.amp: Give [natan] strong drink [shekar] to the one ready to perish [abad -- to be lost, destroyed, dying], and wine [yayin] to those bitter of soul [nephesh -- the life, the inner self].
6.notes: abad (H6) is to perish or be utterly lost; the 'bitter of soul' (nephesh, H5315) are the crushed and dying. Wine that wrecks a king (v. 4) is here a mercy to the suffering -- the same gift, judged entirely by who holds it and why. It is medicine for the dying, not a diet for the ruler.

7.text: Let the cup loose him from his poverty, and let his weary toil press on his mind no longer.
7.amp: Let him drink [shatah] and forget [shakach] his poverty [reysh], and remember [zakar -- call to mind, keep in memory] his misery [amal -- toil, trouble, weary suffering] no longer.
7.notes: amal (H5999) is grinding labor and sorrow -- the same word Ecclesiastes uses for life 'under the sun.' The forgetting wine grants the dying (v. 7) is the very opposite of the forgetting it inflicts on a judge (v. 5): one is relief, the other is dereliction.

8.text: Open your mouth for the voiceless, in the cause of all who are left to ruin.
8.amp: Open [pathach] your mouth [peh] for the mute [illem -- the speechless, the one who cannot plead for himself], in the cause [din] of all the sons of passing-away [those appointed to destruction, left desolate].
8.notes: illem (H483) is the one literally unable to speak -- here standing for all who have no voice in the gate. The king's tongue, kept clear of wine (v. 4), now does its true work: it becomes the voice of those who have none. Power exists to speak for the powerless.

9.text: Open your mouth, judge with righteousness, and defend the cause of the poor and the needy.
9.amp: Open [pathach] your mouth [peh], judge [shaphat -- govern, decide, render a verdict] righteously [tsedek -- in rightness, justice], and plead the cause [din] of the poor [ani -- the afflicted, humble] and the needy [evyon -- the destitute who must beg].
9.notes: shaphat (H8199) is the ruler's defining act, to judge and govern; the oracle ends where royal authority finds its purpose -- tsedek (H6664) for the ani (H6041) and evyon (H34). This closes the charge to Lemuel and turns the page to the woman whose own mouth (v. 26) will likewise open in wisdom.

10.text: A woman of valor -- who can find her? Her worth runs far beyond rubies.
10.amp: A woman [ishshah] of valor [chayil -- strength, might, worth; the warrior's word] -- who can find [matsa] her? Her price [meker -- value, what she is worth] is far [rachoq -- distant, remote] beyond rubies [peninim].
10.notes: the acrostic opens at aleph. chayil (H2428) is not 'virtue' in any dainty sense -- it is the word for an army's strength and a soldier's valor (cf. v. 3); this is a mighty woman. Her worth set 'far beyond rubies' (peninim, H6443) echoes wisdom herself in 3:15 and 8:11 -- she is wisdom made flesh in a household.

11.text: The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will lack no gain.
11.amp: The heart [leb] of her husband [baal -- master, owner, lord of the house] trusts [batach -- relies in full confidence, leans his weight upon] in her, and he will not lack [chaser -- be without, fall short] for spoil [shalal -- plunder, the gain a man wins].
11.notes: batach (H982) is settled, weight-bearing trust -- the same verb used of trusting in the LORD (3:5). shalal (H7998) is usually battle-plunder; with this woman of valor at home, her husband needs no raid for gain -- her industry is his abundance. The warrior imagery is sustained: a wife of chayil wins the spoil.

12.text: She brings him good and never harm, all the days of her life.
12.amp: She deals out [gamal -- renders, repays, brings about] to him good [tov -- what is good, pleasant, beneficial] and not evil [ra -- harm, injury, wrong], all the days [yom] of her life [chay -- her living].
12.notes: gamal (H1580) means to deal out or recompense -- a sustained, deliberate doing of good, not a passing mood. 'All the days of her life' marks it as a lifelong settled disposition, the opposite of the 'strange woman' of chapter 2 whose path runs down to death.

13.text: She seeks out wool and flax, and works it with eager hands.
13.amp: She seeks [darash -- searches out, inquires after] wool [tsemer] and flax [pishteh], and works [asah -- makes, fashions] with the delight [chephets -- pleasure, desire, willing eagerness] of her hands [kaph -- the open palms].
13.notes: darash (H1875) is the diligent seeking of one who studies and pursues; chephets (H2656) means she works not by grim duty but with genuine delight. Wool and flax are the raw stuff of clothing -- she begins at the source and labors with willing hands.

14.text: Like a trader's fleet she is -- carrying home her bread from distant places.
14.amp: Like the trader's [sachar -- one who goes about trafficking, a merchant] ships [oniyyah -- seagoing vessels] she is; she carries home [bo -- brings in, causes to come] her bread [lechem -- food, sustenance] from distant places [merchaq -- a far-off place].
14.notes: sachar (H5503) is the traveling merchant; the image is a fleet of trading vessels crossing the sea for choice cargo. This Israelite homemaker has the reach and enterprise of international commerce -- nothing of the household is too far for her care.

15.text: She rises while it is still night, sets food before her household, and assigns each servant girl her portion.
15.amp: She rises [qum -- gets up, stands] while it is still night [layil], and gives [natan] provision [tereph -- prey, food torn for the table] to her household [bayith], and a portion [choq -- an allotted, decreed share] to her servant girls [naarah -- young women, maidservants].
15.notes: qum (H6965) before dawn marks her diligence; choq (H2706) is an appointed, decreed allotment -- the same root as the 'engraved' law of v. 5. She rules her house with ordered provision, giving each her due before the day's work begins.

16.text: She sizes up a field and acquires it; from the earnings of her hands she plants a vineyard.
16.amp: She considers [zamam -- plans, devises, deliberates carefully] a field [sadeh -- open ground, farmland], and takes [laqach -- receives, acquires] it; from the fruit [periy] of her hands [kaph] she plants [nata -- sets, establishes] a vineyard [kerem].
16.notes: zamam (H2161) is shrewd, deliberate planning -- elsewhere a 'gray' word for plotting, here put to good use (cf. the 'discretion' of 1:4). She is no mere laborer but an investor: she weighs the purchase, buys, and from her own profit establishes a vineyard that will yield for years.

17.text: She girds her waist with strength and makes her arms strong for the work.
17.amp: She girds [chagar -- belts, binds up for action] her loins [mothen -- the waist, the seat of bodily strength] with strength [oz -- might, power], and makes strong [amats -- braces, makes firm and courageous] her arms [zeroa -- the arm, the limb of effort].
17.notes: chagar (H2296) is to gird the loins for vigorous labor or battle; oz (H5797) is power, and amats (H553) is to brace with courage. The warrior language of chayil (v. 10) becomes physical: she rolls up her sleeves and sets her muscle to the task.

18.text: She knows her trading is good; her lamp does not go out at night.
18.amp: She perceives [taam -- tastes, discerns by experience] that her trade [sachar -- her gain, her merchandise] is good [tov]; her lamp [ner] does not go out [kabah -- be quenched, extinguished] by night [layil].
18.notes: taam (H2938) literally means to taste -- she knows the quality of her work by proven experience, not guesswork. The lamp that never goes out signals both her late industry and her household's settled security and welcome; cf. the steady light of the righteous in 13:9.

19.text: She sets her hands to the distaff, and her palms grasp the spindle.
19.amp: She lays [shalach -- sends, reaches out] her hands [yad] to the distaff [kiyshor -- the staff that holds the unspun fiber], and her palms [kaph] take firm hold of [tamak -- grasp, support, sustain] the spindle [pelek -- the whirling weight that twists the thread].
19.notes: tamak (H8551) is to grasp firmly and uphold; kiyshor (H3601) and pelek (H6418) are the tools of spinning thread from raw fiber. The valiant woman's strength of v. 17 turns to skilled, patient handwork -- the same hands that buy fields also spin the thread.

20.text: She opens her palm to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy.
20.amp: She spreads open [paras -- stretches out, extends wide] her palm [kaph] to the poor [ani -- the afflicted, humbled], and reaches out [shalach -- sends forth] her hands [yad] to the needy [evyon -- the destitute].
20.notes: the same outstretched hands that grasp the spindle (v. 19) open wide to the ani (H6041) and evyon (H34) -- the very poor Lemuel's mother charged the king to defend (v. 9). Her industry is not hoarding but the engine of her generosity; what she gathers, she gives.

21.text: She has no fear of the snow for her household, for all of them are clothed in scarlet.
21.amp: She is not afraid [yare -- in dread, anxious] of the snow [sheleg] for her household [bayith], for all her household are clothed [labash -- dressed, wrapped] in scarlet [shaniy -- crimson dye, and so rich double garments].
21.notes: shaniy (H8144) is scarlet, a costly dye; an old reading also hears 'double garments,' warm against the cold. Either way the sense is the same: her forethought has so provisioned the house that winter holds no terror. She does not fear because she has prepared.

22.text: She makes her own coverings; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
22.amp: She makes [asah] for herself coverings [marbad -- spreads, woven coverlets] of tapestry; her clothing [lebush -- garment, attire] is fine linen [shesh] and purple [argaman -- royal purple-crimson].
22.notes: shesh is fine white linen and argaman (H713) the costly purple of royalty (Exod 26:1; Esth 8:15). Having clothed her household (v. 21), she is herself robed in the finest -- not vanity but the fitting dignity of one whose labor has earned it.

23.text: Her husband is known in the gates, when he takes his seat among the elders of the land.
23.amp: Her husband [baal] is known [yada -- recognized, esteemed, known by name] in the gates [shaar -- the city gate, seat of council and court], when he sits [yashab -- takes his seat, dwells] among the elders [zaqen -- old men, the council of the wise] of the land [eretz].
23.notes: the gate (shaar, H8179) was the place of public judgment and civic rule (cf. the 'gate' of the closing verse, v. 31). Her excellence at home lifts her husband's standing in public: he sits among the elders honored, in part, because of the household she has built.

24.text: Garments of woven linen she fashions and sells, and she furnishes the traders with sashes.
24.amp: Fine linen [sadin -- woven linen wraps] she fashions [asah] and sells [makar -- trades it for profit], and she furnishes [natan -- gives, hands over] sashes [chagor -- belts, girdles] to the Canaanite [kenaaniy -- merchant, trader].
24.notes: kenaaniy (H3669) means literally 'Canaanite,' which came to stand for 'merchant,' since Phoenician Canaanites were the era's great traders. She is a producer for the open market -- her enterprise reaches past her own door into commerce and trade.

25.text: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the days to come.
25.amp: Strength [oz -- might, power, and so a place of refuge] and honor [hadar -- splendor, majesty, dignity] are her clothing [lebush]; and she laughs [sachaq -- laughs, rejoices, is merry] at the day [yom] to come [acharon -- the last, the latter, what lies ahead].
25.notes: her true garments are not the linen and purple of v. 22 but oz (H5797) and hadar (H1926) -- strength and dignity. sachaq (H7832) is the confident laughter of one secure against the future; like wisdom, she fears no tomorrow because her house is built and her trust is settled.

26.text: When her mouth opens, wisdom comes forth, and her tongue bears the law of steadfast kindness.
26.amp: When she opens [pathach] her mouth [peh], wisdom [chokmah -- skill in living, the book's master theme] comes forth; and her tongue [lashon] bears the instruction [torah -- teaching, law] of kindness [chesed -- steadfast, covenant-faithful love].
26.notes: her mouth opens (pathach) as the king's was charged to (vv. 8-9) -- but in chokmah (H2451), the wisdom this whole book has sought. torah (H8451) of chesed (H2617): her teaching is law softened by loyal love, the same blend of truth and steadfast kindness that marks God's own covenant word.

27.text: She keeps watch over the ways of her household, and never eats the bread of idleness.
27.amp: She watches over [tsaphah -- keeps watch like a sentinel, a watchman on the wall] the ways [halikah -- the goings, the comings and goings] of her household [bayith], and does not eat [akal] the bread [lechem] of idleness [atsluth -- laziness, sloth].
27.notes: tsaphah (H6822) is the watchman's vigilant looking-out (cf. Ezek 3:17) -- she guards her home as a sentry guards a city. The 'bread of idleness' she refuses is the opposite of the bread she brings from afar (v. 14): she will not feed on sloth.

28.text: Up rise her children to pronounce her blessed; her husband too lifts his voice in her praise:
28.amp: Her children [ben -- her sons and offspring] rise up [qum -- stand up] and call her blessed [ashar -- pronounce her happy, declare her fortunate]; her husband [baal] also, and he praises [halal -- boasts of her, sings her praise] her:
28.notes: ashar (H833) is to call someone blessed or happy -- the same root as the 'Blessed is the man' of Psalm 1:1; halal (H1984) is the strong praise-verb behind Hallelujah. Those who know her best, who live under her daily care, are the ones who rise to crown her with praise.

29.text: 'Many daughters have done valiantly, but you surpass them all.'
29.amp: 'Many [rav -- numerous, abundant] daughters [bath] have done [asah] valiantly [chayil -- with strength and worth, the acrostic's keyword], but you have gone up [alah -- ascended, risen above] over them all.'
29.notes: the husband's praise (begun in v. 28) crowns her with the poem's defining word again -- chayil (H2428): many have shown valor, but she rises above (alah, H5927) them all. It is the verdict the whole acrostic has built toward.

30.text: Charm is a lie and beauty a fleeting breath, but a woman who fears the LORD -- she will be praised.
30.amp: Favor [chen -- charm, grace, outward attractiveness] is deceitful [sheqer -- a falsehood, a lie], and beauty [yophi] is vapor [hebel -- a breath, a vapor, 'vanity' -- the word that rings through Ecclesiastes]; but a woman [ishshah] who fears [yare -- reveres in awe] the LORD [YHWH], she shall be praised [halal].
30.notes: the poem's theological climax: hebel (H1892) is the fleeting breath of Ecclesiastes' 'vanity of vanities,' set against the one durable thing -- the fear of the LORD (yare, H3373). Beauty fades like vapor; the woman who reveres YHWH (H3068) is the one truly praised (halal), and so the book returns to its first principle (1:7).

31.text: Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.amp: Give [natan] her of the fruit [periy] of her hands [yad]; and let her own works [maaseh -- deeds, the things she has made] praise [halal] her in the gates [shaar -- the public square of the city].
31.notes: maaseh (H4639) is her handiwork, the visible product of all her labor; the book ends by sending her own deeds to praise (halal) her in the very gates (shaar, H8179) where her husband is honored (v. 23). She needs no flatterer -- her works speak for her in the place of public judgment, the final word of Proverbs on a life of wisdom.
